name: Quest (query-aware KV page sparsity) - NOT KV quantization
bits: none - no bits reduced. Only the top-K critical KV pages are LOADED for attention; the rest stay in memory but are not read.
activation_scheme: None. Page-level min and max Key values are tracked in the KV cache pages; a query vector estimates each page's criticality and only the top-K pages are fetched for attention. Sparsity, not quantization.
kernels: Quest implementation (mit-han-lab/Quest); designed to reduce the KV-cache LOADING cost that dominates attention at long context.
quality_delta: From the abstract: up to 2.23x self-attention speedup, reducing inference latency by 7.03x, 'while performing well on tasks with long dependencies with negligible accuracy loss'. The 7.03x is inference latency, not attention latency - the attention number is 2.23x.
notes: Recorded to mark the boundary again, and it is a sharp one: Quest is the method that most clearly shows why KV quantization and KV sparsity are different tools. Quest's insight is that token criticality is QUERY-DEPENDENT - a fixed eviction policy like H2O or SnapKV commits in advance to which tokens matter, while Quest picks per query and therefore keeps information that a static policy would have discarded. Consequence for a serving system: quantization is unconditional and always applies, sparsity is selective and only pays off at long context. Both are recorded in the KV family because both answer 'does this request fit', which is why this problem matters as much as weight quantization. SCHEME RECLASSIFIED (parent agent, 2026-10-03): scheme was 'spinquant' (a proxy recorded while the enum lacked a legal value) and is now 'kv-sparsity'.
